READING

**Setting the terms of comparison**

The relevant horizon is the three Vantwyn seasons (2027–2029), after which the lorry loses its vale permit and the equipment question reopens anyway. I will compare the two courses over that window, treating the queen-rearing shed as a shared sunk asset that appears under neither course (Ravensgate buy only the pallets and the lorry).

---

**Annual honey income baseline**

All 640 colonies on own sites last season: £143,000. Per colony that is £223.44. The problem separates out borage at £71 per colony, implying heather accounts for roughly £152 per colony. I will use those component figures below.

---

**Course ORMSCLEUCH – three-year revenue**

All 640 colonies on heather and borage throughout.

| Item | Annual | 3-year total |
|---|---|---|
| Heather and borage, 640 colonies | £143,000 | £429,000 |
| Equipment sale (2026, once) | £96,000 | £96,000 |
| **Total** | | **£525,000** |

No haulage, no spray losses. Colonies undisturbed for the full season every year.

---

**Course TREVANNOCK – three-year revenue**

400 colonies go to Vantwyn in April each year; they return too late for Kirkhallow borage but in time for heather. 240 colonies remain on own sites throughout.

*Honey income:*
- 240 colonies, full season (heather + borage): 240 × £223.44 = **£53,625**
- 400 colonies, heather only after return: 400 × £152 = **£60,800**

*Pollination income:*
- 400 × £168 = **£67,200**

*Costs – spray losses:*
- 9% of 400 = 36 colonies × £210 replacement = **–£7,560**

*Costs – haulage and labour:*
- **–£6,900**

**Annual net under TREVANNOCK: £167,165**

Over three seasons: **£501,495**

Equipment residual at end of 2029 (permit gone 2030-01-01): **~£20,000**

**TREVANNOCK three-year total: £521,495**

---

**Direct comparison**

| Course | 3-year total | Advantage |
|---|---|---|
| ORMSCLEUCH | £525,000 | +£3,505 |
| TREVANNOCK | £521,495 | – |

The gap is narrow undiscounted. Once you apply even a modest time-value adjustment, it widens in ORMSCLEUCH's favour, because ORMSCLEUCH puts £96,000 into hand in late 2026 while TREVANNOCK's operational premium of roughly £24,000 per year arrives across 2027–2029 and its £20,000 equipment residual arrives last of all.

Put differently: the operational advantage of TREVANNOCK over three years (≈£73,000 undiscounted) falls short of the equipment gap it sacrifices (£96,000 now versus £20,000 in three years = £76,000 differential). TREVANNOCK never recoups within the life of the contract.

---

**Risk under TREVANNOCK**

The 9% mortality figure is a single data point – Whinnerdale's experience in 2025 on the same spray programme. Vantwyn will not vary that programme. If losses ran at 12%, the annual net falls by another £1,890; at 15%, by another £5,040. The risk is entirely absorbed by Thistledown and there is no contractual remedy. A bad spray year also weakens surviving colonies and their honey yield in subsequent seasons, a second-order cost that is not in the headline figures.

---

**The Coldharbour and Nyefield factor**

Two vale growers have asked for a 2028 quote. This is the strongest argument for TREVANNOCK: it keeps market presence alive. But consider the practicalities:

1. In 2028 all 400 allocated colonies are already committed to Vantwyn. Unless Thistledown expands, there is nothing spare to offer.
2. Any vale contract from 2030 onward would be hampered by the lorry's permit loss. The equipment that makes those contracts viable is heading toward a £20,000 scrap value by the time the permit falls away.
3. The business already tested migratory pollination fully – three contracts, all three lapsed, £187,000 of capital deployed with no renewal. Coldharbour and Nyefield are enquiries, not offers, from a market where Thistledown has just demonstrated that retention is difficult.

The optionality has real value, but it is not large enough to overturn the arithmetic.

---

**What happens after 2029**

Under ORMSCLEUCH, the business from 2030 onwards is exactly what it was in 2024: 640 colonies, own sites, heather and borage, no external dependency. Under TREVANNOCK, Thistledown exits 2029 holding a lorry worth £20,000 as a farm vehicle, pallets whose resale value after three more years of wear is unknown, and a dependence on future contracts that the current contract cycle has not reliably produced. The post-contract position is weaker, not stronger.

---

**Summary**

ORMSCLEUCH wins by roughly £3,500 over three years on an undiscounted basis and by rather more once the early receipt of £96,000 is recognised. It eliminates spray-loss risk, halves operational complexity, and leaves the business in a clean position after 2029. TREVANNOCK does not cover the equipment-value gap it surrenders, carries real biological risk on a spray programme it cannot influence, and ends in 2029 with depreciated kit and no guaranteed continuation.

---

CALL
  ORMSCLEUCH

GROUNDS
  The £76,000 equipment-value gap between selling now (£96,000) and holding to permit-expiry (£20,000) exceeds the entire three-year operational premium that TREVANNOCK generates (≈£73,000 undiscounted), so the Vantwyn contract never returns what it costs in forgone sale proceeds, and that imbalance only deepens once the earlier receipt of sale funds is discounted.
